laws.title: Firearms Act — Restricted and Prohibited Weapons
laws.subtitle: Handguns restricted; automatic weapons prohibited; PAL required for any firearm
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Firearms Act (SC 1995 c 39) classifies firearms as non-restricted, restricted, or prohibited. Handguns are restricted; automatic weapons and many semi-automatics are prohibited. Visitors cannot import restricted or prohibited firearms. Non-restricted long guns require a valid PAL (Possession and Acquisition Licence). Since 2020, the government has banned over 1,500 models of assault-style firearms. Storage regulations require trigger locks and secure storage.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment for unauthorized possession of restricted firearm
laws.exceptions: Licensed hunters and sport shooters may transport restricted firearms under strict ATT (Authorization to Transport) conditions

quiz.q: Which Canadian law classifies firearms as restricted or prohibited?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Cannabis Act 2018 — Possession Limits and Border Rules
laws.subtitle: 30g public limit legal; crossing ANY border with cannabis is criminal regardless
laws.fullDescription: The Cannabis Act (SC 2018 c 16) legalized recreational cannabis federally. Adults (19+ in most provinces, 18+ in Alberta) may possess up to 30 grams in public. Home cultivation of up to 4 plants permitted federally. Crossing borders with cannabis to or from US states where it is legal remains a serious federal criminal offence. CBSA officers specifically ask about cannabis at land crossings.
laws.penalty: Up to 14 years for trafficking; summary conviction for minor possession violations
laws.exceptions: Medical cannabis patients with Health Canada authorization may possess larger amounts

quiz.q: Is it legal to bring cannabis across the Canadian-US border even to a legal US state?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Hate Speech (s.319)
laws.subtitle: Public incitement of hatred against identifiable groups is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 319 of the Criminal Code prohibits public statements that wilfully promote hatred against an identifiable group (defined by race, religion, national or ethnic origin, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or disability). Truth and good-faith discussion are narrow defences. Social media posts by visitors have led to border refusals. Canada is stricter than the US on hate speech; the Charter's guarantee of expression is not absolute.
laws.penalty: Up to 2 years imprisonment for wilfully promoting hatred
laws.exceptions: Private conversations; good-faith discussion of public interest matters

quiz.q: Canada's hate speech prohibition falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Controlled Drugs and Substances Act — Drug Trafficking
laws.subtitle: Trafficking fentanyl or heroin carries up to life imprisonment; BC partial decrim
laws.fullDescription: The Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (SC 1996 c 19) governs narcotics. Schedule I substances (heroin, cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine) carry the harshest penalties. Trafficking fentanyl has driven a national overdose crisis with over 40,000 deaths since 2016. British Columbia piloted decriminalization (Jan 2023-Jan 2026) for personal amounts of some drugs, but possession remains a federal offence elsewhere.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment for trafficking Schedule I drugs; 7 years for possession for purpose of trafficking
laws.exceptions: British Columbia pilot decriminalization for personal amounts only; medical prescription exemptions

quiz.q: Canada's drug trafficking law falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Impaired Driving — Criminal Code s.320.14
laws.subtitle: 0.08 BAC criminal; 0.05 BAC triggers provincial suspensions in most provinces
laws.fullDescription: Section 320.14 of the Criminal Code makes operating a motor vehicle while impaired by alcohol or drugs an indictable offence. The per se limit is 80mg/100mL blood alcohol. Most provinces impose administrative licence suspensions at 0.05 BAC. Cannabis-impaired driving is equally illegal; police use standardized field sobriety tests and oral fluid testing. Since 2018, refusing a breathalyzer test is treated the same as being over the legal limit.
laws.penalty: First offence: $1,000 minimum fine; repeat offences up to life imprisonment if death caused
laws.exceptions: None — there is no safe level of impairment for driving

quiz.q: Canada's impaired driving law falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Distracted Driving — Handheld Device Ban
laws.subtitle: Handheld phone use while driving banned in all provinces; fines up to $3,000
laws.fullDescription: All Canadian provinces and territories ban handheld electronic device use while driving. Ontario's Highway Traffic Act, BC's Motor Vehicle Act, and their counterparts impose fines ranging from $300 to $3,000 and demerit points. A second distracted driving offence in Ontario results in a 7-day licence suspension. Hands-free devices are generally permitted. Watching video content on any screen while driving is prohibited.
laws.penalty: $300-$3,000 fine; 3-6 demerit points; possible licence suspension on repeat offence
laws.exceptions: Hands-free device operation; genuine 911 emergency calls

quiz.q: Canada's distracted driving laws fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Zero-BAC for Young and Novice Drivers
laws.subtitle: Drivers under 21 or with learner licences must have zero BAC in all provinces
laws.fullDescription: All Canadian provinces impose zero-tolerance alcohol policies on novice drivers. In Ontario, G1 and G2 licence holders must have 0.00 BAC. British Columbia requires zero BAC for drivers under 19. The same zero-tolerance applies to cannabis for new drivers. Violations result in immediate 24-hour roadside suspension and additional penalties even below the 0.05 provincial threshold.
laws.penalty: Immediate roadside suspension; fines; possible criminal charge if above 0.08
laws.exceptions: None for novice drivers

quiz.q: Zero-BAC rules for young Canadian drivers fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Seatbelt Laws — All Occupants Mandatory
laws.subtitle: All occupants must be buckled; child car seat rules are strict and provincial
laws.fullDescription: All Canadian provinces mandate seatbelt use for every vehicle occupant. Child car seat requirements vary: rear-facing seats to approximately 9kg, forward-facing to 18kg, then booster seats. Quebec requires booster seats until age 9 or 36kg. Fines apply to the driver for any unbelted passenger under 16. Police conduct regular seatbelt blitzes. Ontario issues $240+ fines per unbelted occupant.
laws.penalty: $200-$500 fines; demerit points; driver responsible for unbelted passengers under 16
laws.exceptions: Medical exemptions with physician certificate

quiz.q: Canada's seatbelt laws fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Winter Tires — Mandatory in Quebec and BC Corridors
laws.subtitle: Quebec requires winter tires Dec 1 to Mar 15; BC requires them on designated mountain routes
laws.fullDescription: Quebec mandates winter tires (marked with the mountain/snowflake symbol) on all passenger vehicles from December 1 to March 15. British Columbia requires winter tires or chains on many highway corridors including the Coquihalla (Hwy 5) and portions of Hwy 3 year-round when the Snowflake sign is displayed. Non-compliant vehicles can be turned back. Rental cars must comply with the same requirements.
laws.penalty: $200-$300 fine in Quebec; BC fines up to $109 plus potential liability if at-fault in an accident
laws.exceptions: All-season tires with M+S rating partially accepted in some BC zones

quiz.q: Winter tire requirements in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: eTA — Electronic Travel Authorization
laws.subtitle: Required for all visa-exempt nationals flying to Canada; USD equivalent CAD $7
laws.fullDescription: Since 2016, citizens of visa-exempt countries (EU, UK, Australia, Japan, etc.) must obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) before boarding a flight to Canada. The eTA costs CAD $7, is usually approved within minutes, and is valid for 5 years or until passport expiry. US citizens are exempt but require a valid passport. Arriving without an eTA results in denied boarding at the departure airport.
laws.penalty: Denied boarding; return flight costs at passenger's own expense
laws.exceptions: US citizens; Canadian permanent residents; those with valid Canadian visa

quiz.q: The Canadian eTA requirement falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Inadmissibility — DUI Can Bar Entry to Canada
laws.subtitle: A single DUI conviction abroad may make you inadmissible since 2018 reclassification
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act deems persons criminally inadmissible for offences equivalent to Canadian indictable offences. Since 2018, impaired driving (DUI) became a hybrid indictable offence in Canada — meaning a DUI conviction in the US or elsewhere may render a visitor inadmissible. Thousands of Americans are turned back at the border each year. A Temporary Resident Permit (TRP) or Criminal Rehabilitation application is required.
laws.penalty: Denied entry; possible detention; return at own expense
laws.exceptions: Criminal Rehabilitation (5+ years after sentence completion) or TRP application approved in advance

quiz.q: Criminal inadmissibility rules for entering Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: CBSA — Currency Declaration over CAD $10,000
laws.subtitle: All currency and monetary instruments over $10,000 must be declared at the border
laws.fullDescription: Under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, anyone crossing Canada's border with CAD $10,000 or more in currency or monetary instruments must declare it to CBSA. This applies to cash, cheques, money orders, and traveller's cheques in any currency. Failure to declare results in seizure of ALL funds (not just the excess). Structuring to avoid the threshold is also an offence.
laws.penalty: Seizure and forfeiture of all funds; fines up to $5,000; possible criminal charges
laws.exceptions: Declaring fully satisfies the requirement; funds may be legally brought in once declared

quiz.q: Canada's currency declaration requirement falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: CBSA Food, Plant, and Animal Import Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Many foods must be declared; undeclared items may be seized and fined
laws.fullDescription: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) restricts import of many food items to prevent agricultural pests. Visitors must declare all food, plants, and animal products on CBSA declaration cards. Fresh fruits, vegetables, meats, and soil from certain countries may be confiscated. Travellers from countries with African swine fever face heightened scrutiny regarding pork products. Fines apply for undeclared items.
laws.penalty: Fines from $200 to $1,300 for agricultural violations; goods confiscated
laws.exceptions: CFIA-approved commercially packaged items; duty-free purchased items within limits

quiz.q: Food import restrictions at the Canadian border fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Working Without Authorization — IRPA Violation
laws.subtitle: Working on a tourist visa is a serious immigration violation
laws.fullDescription: Working in Canada without a valid work permit is prohibited under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Visitors on tourist visas cannot be employed. The open work permit (for spouses of skilled workers), CUSMA/USMCA provisions, and some permit-exempt business activities are exceptions. Employers hiring unauthorized foreign workers face fines up to $1,000,000 per violation under a 2015 amendment.
laws.penalty: Removal from Canada; 1-5 year re-entry ban; fines for employers up to $1,000,000
laws.exceptions: Business visitors for meetings, conferences; certain CUSMA/USMCA professional categories

quiz.q: Unauthorized work in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Species at Risk Act — Wildlife Protection
laws.subtitle: Killing or possessing over 800 listed species carries major criminal penalties
laws.fullDescription: The Species at Risk Act (SC 2002 c 29) prohibits killing, harming, harassing, capturing, or possessing listed wildlife. Canada has 800+ species at risk including polar bears, caribou, beluga whales, woodland caribou, and numerous bird species. The Act applies to federal lands; provinces have complementary legislation. Trophies from protected species cannot be exported. Accidental harm during construction requires mitigation plans.
laws.penalty: Up to $1 million fine and 5 years imprisonment for individuals
laws.exceptions: Aboriginal peoples exercising treaty rights; scientific research with SARA permits

quiz.q: Canada's Species at Risk Act falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Fisheries Act — Habitat Protection and Pollution Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Depositing deleterious substances in fish-bearing waters is prohibited
laws.fullDescription: The Fisheries Act (RSC 1985 c F-14) prohibits depositing deleterious substances in waters frequented by fish. Industrial effluent, agricultural runoff, and improperly disposed motor oil near waterways are all covered. The 2019 amendments restored habitat protections removed in 2012 and added fish passage requirements for dams. DFO officers patrol waterways and prosecute violations. Industrial violations receive the harshest penalties.
laws.penalty: Up to $6 million per day for first-time corporate offenders; up to $2 million for individuals
laws.exceptions: Authorized deposit permits; natural background processes

quiz.q: The Canadian Fisheries Act habitat protection falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Canadian Environmental Protection Act (CEPA) 1999
laws.subtitle: CEPA controls over 4,000 substances; major polluters face criminal sanctions
laws.fullDescription: The Canadian Environmental Protection Act 1999 (SC 1999 c 33) is Canada's primary federal environmental law governing toxic substances, air pollutants, marine pollution, and hazardous waste. Amendments in 2023 (Bill S-5) added rights-based language recognizing the right to a healthy environment. The Environmental Registry must publish environmental protection action plans. Enforcement includes compliance orders and criminal prosecution.
laws.penalty: Up to $1 million per day for corporations; up to $1 million and 3 years for individuals
laws.exceptions: Regulated substances with valid permits; naturally occurring substances at background levels

quiz.q: Canada's CEPA pollution law falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Single-Use Plastics Prohibition Regulations 2022
laws.subtitle: Six single-use plastic categories banned; manufacture, import, and sale prohibited
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Single-Use Plastics Prohibition Regulations (SOR/2022-138) ban manufacture, import, and sale of six single-use plastic items: checkout bags, cutlery, foodservice ware made from problematic plastics, ring carriers, stir sticks, and straws (with some exceptions). Made under CEPA 1999. Some provinces (Ontario, BC) have additional restrictions. Courts struck down parts of the regulation but most provisions remain in force.
laws.penalty: Compliance orders; fines for commercial violations
laws.exceptions: Straws permitted for medical necessity; certain flexible straws for mobility impairment

quiz.q: Canada's single-use plastics ban falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Migratory Birds Convention Act — Bird Protection
laws.subtitle: Migratory birds and their nests protected; lead shot banned for waterfowl hunting
laws.fullDescription: The Migratory Birds Convention Act 1994 (SC 1994 c 22) implements the Canada-US Migratory Birds Convention and protects over 1,000 bird species. Disturbing active nests, collecting eggs, or killing protected birds without a permit is illegal. Farmers and homeowners must survey for nesting before clearing trees or demolishing buildings during breeding season. Non-toxic shot (steel, bismuth) is required for migratory bird hunting; lead shot prohibited.
laws.penalty: Up to $100,000 fine for individuals; up to $1 million for corporations
laws.exceptions: Indigenous peoples with treaty rights; licensed hunters with federal Migratory Game Bird Hunting Permit

quiz.q: Protection of migratory birds in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Nuclear Safety and Control Act — Radioactive Materials
laws.subtitle: CNSC licences required for all nuclear activities; unauthorized possession is criminal
laws.fullDescription: The Nuclear Safety and Control Act (SC 1997 c 9) establishes the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) and requires licences for all nuclear activities including possessing, using, or transporting nuclear substances. Canada is a major uranium producer (Saskatchewan Athabasca Basin) and operates CANDU reactors. Unauthorized import of radioactive material through border crossings triggers serious criminal charges. CNSC maintains the radiation device registry.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment; unlimited fines
laws.exceptions: Medical radioisotopes used in hospitals; licensed nuclear facilities

quiz.q: Nuclear safety regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act — Federal Carbon Tax
laws.subtitle: Carbon price CAD $65/tonne in 2024, rising to $170/tonne by 2030
laws.fullDescription: The Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act (SC 2018 c 12) establishes Canada's federal carbon pricing backstop applied in provinces without equivalent systems. The carbon price reached CAD $65/tonne CO2e in April 2024. An industrial Output-Based Pricing System (OBPS) applies to large emitters. The Supreme Court upheld the Act's constitutionality in 2021. The federal government paused the consumer carbon price on home heating oil in 2023 following political pressure.
laws.penalty: Administrative monetary penalties for non-compliance with industrial OBPS requirements
laws.exceptions: Some agriculture fuel uses; fishing vessels; northern and remote communities

quiz.q: Canada's carbon pricing system falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Canada Labour Code — Federal Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: Federal minimum wage $17.30/hour (2024); provinces set their own rates
laws.fullDescription: The Canada Labour Code (RSC 1985 c L-2) governs workers in federally regulated industries (banking, airlines, rail, telecom). The federal minimum wage is adjusted annually with CPI — $17.30/hour as of April 2024. Provincially regulated workers (the majority) are covered by provincial employment standards: rates range from $14.50 (New Brunswick) to $17.40 (BC). Many cities have living wage campaigns pushing for $20-$25/hour in urban centres.
laws.penalty: Back pay orders; fines for employers under federal and provincial employment standards legislation
laws.exceptions: Student minimum wages exist in some provinces; agricultural workers have reduced coverage

quiz.q: Canada's minimum wage law falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Employment Insurance — Maternity and Parental Benefits
laws.subtitle: Up to 78 weeks combined maternity and parental benefits available through EI
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Employment Insurance Act (SC 1996 c 23) provides 15 weeks maternity benefits and up to 40 standard or 69 extended weeks of parental benefits. Combined, a family can receive up to 78 weeks of EI benefits. Quebec has its own superior Quebec Parental Insurance Plan (RQAP) with higher rates and shorter qualifying periods. The federal benefit rate is 55% of insurable earnings up to the maximum insurable amount ($63,200 in 2024).
laws.penalty: Repayment of EI benefits if fraudulently claimed; additional criminal penalties for fraud
laws.exceptions: Self-employed workers can voluntarily opt into EI; Quebec residents use RQAP

quiz.q: Parental leave benefits in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Occupational Health and Safety — Three Fundamental Rights
laws.subtitle: Workers have the right to know, to participate, and to refuse unsafe work
laws.fullDescription: Both federal (Canada Labour Code Part II) and provincial OHS legislation codify three fundamental worker rights: to know about hazards (WHMIS/GHS labelling), to participate in OHS committees, and to refuse unsafe work without reprisal. Ontario's Occupational Health and Safety Act imposes significant fines on employers after the Westray mine disaster provisions (Bill C-45, 2004) created corporate criminal liability for workplace safety failures. WorkSafe BC regulates BC workers.
laws.penalty: Stop-work orders; fines up to $1.5 million provincially; imprisonment for willful violations causing death
laws.exceptions: Some farm workers and domestic workers have limited coverage in some provinces

quiz.q: Workplace safety rights for Canadian workers fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Canadian Human Rights Act — Workplace Discrimination
laws.subtitle: 13 protected grounds; accommodation to point of undue hardship required
laws.fullDescription: The Canadian Human Rights Act (RSC 1985 c H-6) prohibits discrimination in employment and services under federal jurisdiction on 13 grounds including race, sex, age, disability, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, and marital status. The Canadian Human Rights Commission investigates; the Tribunal adjudicates. Harassment constitutes discrimination. Employers must accommodate to the point of undue hardship (significant cost or risk to safety).
laws.penalty: Compensation for lost wages and pain and suffering; reinstatement orders; public interest orders
laws.exceptions: Bona fide occupational requirement (BFOR) defence available to employers

quiz.q: Anti-discrimination protections in Canadian federal workplaces fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Pay Equity Act 2018 — Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value
laws.subtitle: Federal employers with 10+ employees must conduct proactive pay equity analyses
laws.fullDescription: The Pay Equity Act (SC 2018 c 27), in force since August 2021, requires federally regulated employers with 10+ employees to establish pay equity plans comparing compensation for jobs predominantly done by women versus men. Plans must be posted, updated every 5 years, and reported to the Pay Equity Commissioner. Quebec's Pay Equity Act (since 1996) has similar requirements for provincially regulated employers.
laws.penalty: Compliance orders; administrative monetary penalties up to $50,000
laws.exceptions: Employers under 10 employees; non-federal employers covered by provincial legislation

quiz.q: Pay equity requirements for Canadian employers fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Canada Pension Plan — Mandatory Contributions
laws.subtitle: CPP contributions mandatory for all employed Canadians 18-70 outside Quebec
laws.fullDescription: The Canada Pension Plan (RSC 1985 c C-8) is a mandatory contributory retirement pension for employed Canadians aged 18-70 (Quebec uses QPP). In 2024, employees contribute 5.95% of earnings between $3,500 and $68,500; employers match this amount. Enhanced CPP2 contributions apply on earnings up to $73,200. Self-employed pay both shares but may deduct the employer portion for tax. CRA aggressively enforces remittance obligations.
laws.penalty: 10% penalty on late CPP remittances; interest at prescribed rate; directors personally liable
laws.exceptions: Quebec workers use QPP; certain religious orders have exemptions

quiz.q: Canada Pension Plan contributions fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Weapons Offences: Prohibited Items (s.88-96)
laws.subtitle: Switchblades, push daggers, brass knuckles, and pepper spray are prohibited weapons
laws.fullDescription: Sections 88-96 of the Criminal Code prohibit carrying concealed weapons and possessing prohibited weapons. Prohibited weapons include switchblades, butterfly knives, push daggers, brass knuckles, nunchaku, and ninja stars. Pepper spray is classified as a prohibited weapon in Canada — unlike the US — and possession without a Firearms Licence (PAL) is illegal. Bear banger launchers require registration. Many tourists are unaware these items are prohibited.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years for prohibited weapon possession; up to 5 years for concealed weapon
laws.exceptions: Law enforcement; licensed collectors with proper permits

quiz.q: Prohibited weapons possession in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Unauthorized Computer Access (s.342.1)
laws.subtitle: Hacking or fraudulently obtaining computer services is an indictable offence
laws.fullDescription: Section 342.1 of the Criminal Code prohibits fraudulently obtaining computer services, intercepting computer data, or using computer systems to commit fraud. Canada has signed the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime. The Act covers unauthorized access to Wi-Fi networks, exploiting software vulnerabilities, and using others' passwords without authorization. Hacking government or critical infrastructure systems faces enhanced prosecution under s.430.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment
laws.exceptions: Authorized penetration testing with written permission from system owner

quiz.q: Unauthorized computer access in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Non-Consensual Intimate Image Distribution (s.162.1)
laws.subtitle: Sharing intimate images without consent is criminal — added 2014 in response to cyberbullying cases
laws.fullDescription: Section 162.1 of the Criminal Code, added in 2014 following the Rehtaeh Parsons and Amanda Todd cyberbullying cases, criminalizes non-consensual distribution of intimate images. The offence covers sharing, publishing, transmitting, or advertising intimate images knowing the subject did not consent or being reckless about consent. Victims can obtain peace bonds and civil remedies. Multiple provinces have complementary civil legislation.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment; mandatory publication ban protecting victim's identity
laws.exceptions: Images used for law enforcement investigation under court warrant

quiz.q: Non-consensual intimate image sharing in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Proceeds of Crime — Money Laundering (PCMLTFA)
laws.subtitle: Cash over $10,000 reported; structuring transactions to avoid reporting is criminal
laws.fullDescription: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (SC 2000 c 17) requires financial entities to report cash transactions over $10,000 CAD and suspicious transactions of any amount to FINTRAC. Canada has faced international criticism for real estate money laundering (snow-washing) particularly in Vancouver and Toronto. A federal inquiry (Cullen Commission) in BC concluded in 2022 finding systemic failures. Structuring transactions to avoid reporting is criminal.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for money laundering; up to life imprisonment for terrorist financing
laws.exceptions: None — suspicious transaction reporting is mandatory regardless of amount

quiz.q: Canada's anti-money laundering law falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Anti-Terrorism Act — Criminal Code Part II.1
laws.subtitle: Participating in or financing terrorist activity carries life imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Part II.1 of the Criminal Code (added post-9/11, strengthened by Anti-terrorism Act 2015) defines terrorist activity and creates terrorism offences including participation in terrorist groups, facilitating terrorism, and hoarding weapons for terrorist purposes. Canada experienced attacks in 2014 (Parliament Hill, Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu) and has prosecuted returning foreign fighters. CSIS and RCMP coordinate investigations. The Secure Air Travel Act (no-fly list) operates under this framework.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment for most terrorism offences
laws.exceptions: None — lawful protest and dissent are not terrorism if peaceful

quiz.q: Terrorism offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Human Trafficking (s.279.01)
laws.subtitle: Trafficking minors carries up to life imprisonment; Canada is destination and transit country
laws.fullDescription: Section 279.01 of the Criminal Code makes recruiting, transporting, or controlling a person for exploitation an indictable offence carrying up to life imprisonment for victims under 18. Canada is both a destination and transit country for human trafficking, with most domestic trafficking involving Canadian-born victims in urban sex industry contexts. The National Human Trafficking Hotline (1-833-900-1010) is available 24/7.
laws.penalty: Up to life imprisonment for trafficking minors; up to 14 years for adult victims
laws.exceptions: None — consent is not a defence to human trafficking

quiz.q: Human trafficking in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Stalking and Criminal Harassment (s.264)
laws.subtitle: Repeatedly following, contacting, or threatening a person to cause fear is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 264 of the Criminal Code makes criminal harassment illegal — repeatedly following, communicating with, or watching a person or their family members such that they fear for their safety. Online stalking and cyberstalking fall under this provision. Domestic violence criminal harassment is a significant driver of prosecutions. A recognizance (peace bond) may be issued pre-charge if harassment is feared.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment on indictment; up to 18 months on summary conviction
laws.exceptions: Lawful police surveillance; authorized process serving

quiz.q: Criminal harassment (stalking) in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Gambling Regulations (s.201-206)
laws.subtitle: Single-game sports betting legalized 2021; unlicensed gambling operations criminal
laws.fullDescription: Canada legalized single-game sports betting in 2021 (Bill C-218). Provincial lottery corporations (OLG, BCLC, Loto-Quebec) operate legal online betting platforms. Operating an unlicensed gambling operation (common gaming house) is criminal under s.201-206. Most provinces run licensed casinos. Indigenous gaming compacts allow reserve casinos. Online gambling through unlicensed offshore sites is technically illegal but rarely prosecuted for individual players.
laws.penalty: Up to 2 years for keeping a common gaming house
laws.exceptions: Licensed provincial gaming corporations; social gambling with no house rake

quiz.q: Gambling regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Break and Enter (s.348)
laws.subtitle: Breaking into a dwelling-house carries up to life imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Section 348 of the Criminal Code makes breaking and entering with intent to commit an indictable offence in a dwelling-house punishable by up to life imprisonment. Entry into commercial spaces carries up to 10 years. The offence does not require forced entry — remaining after authorization is withdrawn constitutes the offence. Aggravated home invasion (with weapon or while wearing disguise) is prosecuted under s.348.1 with additional penalties.
laws.penalty: Up to life imprisonment for dwelling-house break-and-enter; up to 10 years for other places
laws.exceptions: Lawful entry; entry by owner; lawful execution of warrants

quiz.q: Break and enter offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Fraud and False Pretences (s.380)
laws.subtitle: Fraud over $5,000 carries up to 14 years; identity fraud addressed separately
laws.fullDescription: Section 380 of the Criminal Code makes fraud (dishonest act or omission causing deprivation by deceit, falsehood, or other fraudulent means) criminal. Fraud over $5,000 carries up to 14 years; under $5,000 is a hybrid offence up to 2 years. Market manipulation is a specific subtype. Identity theft (s.402.2) and identity fraud (s.403) add further layers. Canada Revenue Agency fraud (tax evasion) is prosecuted under both the ITA and Criminal Code.
laws.penalty: Up to 14 years for fraud over $5,000; additional charges for identity fraud
laws.exceptions: Good faith mistaken belief may negate dishonest intent

quiz.q: Fraud offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: PIPEDA — Personal Data Protection and Privacy
laws.subtitle: Organizations must protect personal data; breach notification mandatory since 2018
laws.fullDescription: PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, SC 2000 c 5) requires organizations to obtain consent for data collection and to safeguard personal information. Since 2018, significant breach notifications must be sent to the OPC and affected individuals. Quebec's Law 25 (in force 2022-2023) is stricter than PIPEDA with fines up to $25 million or 4% of global revenue. Proposed Bill C-27 (Consumer Privacy Protection Act) would replace PIPEDA with stronger federal rules.
laws.penalty: Up to $100,000 fines for breaches under PIPEDA; up to $25 million under Quebec Law 25
laws.exceptions: Journalistic, artistic, and literary purposes; personal or domestic use

quiz.q: Personal data protection law in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Canada Elections Act — Electoral Offences
laws.subtitle: Voter fraud, impersonation, and foreign interference in elections are criminal
laws.fullDescription: The Canada Elections Act (SC 2000 c 9) prohibits voter fraud, ballot tampering, impersonating voters, and foreign interference in elections. The Elections Modernization Act 2018 specifically prohibited foreign third-party spending on partisan activities during pre-writ periods. A 2022-2024 public inquiry into Chinese foreign interference in the 2019 and 2021 federal elections concluded interference occurred. Campaigning within 1km of a polling station on election day is prohibited.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for serious electoral fraud; fines up to $50,000 for third-party spending violations
laws.exceptions: Authorized candidates and parties within regulated spending limits

quiz.q: Electoral fraud offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: National Parks Act — Parks Canada Regulations
laws.subtitle: Feeding wildlife, off-trail travel, campfire violations carry heavy fines
laws.fullDescription: The Canada National Parks Act (SC 2000 c 32) and Parks Canada regulations prohibit feeding wildlife (a bear habituated to human food is euthanized — the park says "a fed bear is a dead bear"), picking plants, removing rocks or fossils, using drones without permits, and setting campfires outside designated areas. Jasper and Banff have wildlife corridor closures during elk and grizzly bear seasons. Backcountry camping requires advance reservation and bear canister.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $25,000 for wildlife disturbance; $5,000 for prohibited campfires
laws.exceptions: Authorized research permits; Indigenous peoples accessing traditional lands

quiz.q: National park wildlife and fire regulations fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Copyright Act — Intellectual Property
laws.subtitle: Copyright automatic on creation; life + 70 years since 2022 CUSMA extension
laws.fullDescription: The Copyright Act (RSC 1985 c C-42) provides automatic protection to original works for the life of the author plus 70 years (extended from 50 years by CUSMA/USMCA agreement effective 2022). Commercial copyright infringement is criminal. Canada's notice-and-notice regime (not US-style notice-and-takedown) requires ISPs to forward infringement notices. Fair dealing for research, education, satire, and parody is a Canadian defence (broader than US fair use in educational contexts).
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for commercial copyright infringement; civil damages up to $20,000 non-commercial
laws.exceptions: Fair dealing for research, private study, education, satire, parody; news reporting

quiz.q: Copyright protection in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Animal Cruelty (s.445-447.1)
laws.subtitle: Wilfully causing unnecessary pain to animals is criminal; up to 5 years for willful cruelty
laws.fullDescription: Sections 445-447.1 of the Criminal Code address animal cruelty. Wilfully causing unnecessary pain, suffering, or injury to animals, killing without lawful excuse, or abandoning an animal in distress are criminal offences. Dog fighting and cockfighting carry up to 5 years. Provincial SPCAs (Humane Societies) have enforcement authority. Several high-profile cases involving farmed animals have raised questions about exemptions for standard agricultural practices.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for willful animal cruelty; up to 2 years for neglect
laws.exceptions: Lawful hunting with proper licences; veterinary procedures; farm practices following industry standards

quiz.q: Animal cruelty offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Commercial Vehicles — Hours of Service Regulations
laws.subtitle: Electronic logging devices mandatory since 2023; 13-hour daily driving limit
laws.fullDescription: Transport Canada's Commercial Vehicle Drivers Hours of Service Regulations (SOR/2005-313) limit commercial truck and bus drivers to 13 hours of driving in a 24-hour period with mandatory rest requirements. Electronic logging devices (ELDs) became mandatory for federally regulated carriers in January 2023. Roadside inspections use CVSA protocols. Violations result in out-of-service orders and fines. Canada and the US have partially harmonized their HOS rules for cross-border trucking.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $3,000 for drivers; up to $10,000 for carriers per violation
laws.exceptions: Short-distance exemptions; agricultural transport during harvest season

quiz.q: Commercial driver hours of service regulations fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Motorcycle Helmet Laws — All Provinces Mandatory
laws.subtitle: CSA- or DOT-certified helmets required for all motorcycle riders and passengers
laws.fullDescription: All Canadian provinces mandate approved helmet use by motorcycle operators and passengers. Helmets must meet CMVSS 218 or equivalent standards (DOT, ECE 22-05). Manitoba provides a $50 helmet rebate. Riding without a compliant helmet results in fines and demerit points. Open-face helmets are legal but full-face helmets are recommended. Motorcycle endorsement (M class licence) required to operate a motorcycle; graduated licensing applies in most provinces.
laws.penalty: $100-$500 fines; demerit points; insurance implications
laws.exceptions: Manitoba special provision for Hutterite communities on religious grounds

quiz.q: Motorcycle helmet laws in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Speed Limits — Provincial Rules and Photo Radar
laws.subtitle: Urban default 50km/h; school zones 30km/h; photo radar active in most provinces
laws.fullDescription: Canadian speed limits are provincially set. Urban areas default to 50km/h; residential zones often 40km/h; school and playground zones 30km/h when children present. Highway limits range from 100-130km/h. Photo radar and automated speed enforcement cameras operate in Alberta, Ontario, BC, and other provinces. Construction zones carry double fines. Speeding 50+km/h over the limit triggers roadside licence suspension in Ontario.
laws.penalty: Fines $2.50-$9.75/km over limit in Ontario; demerit points; immediate suspension for extreme speed
laws.exceptions: Emergency vehicles on active calls; designated racing events on closed circuits

quiz.q: Speed limit laws in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Cycling Regulations — Helmets and E-bike Rules
laws.subtitle: Bike helmets mandatory for all cyclists in BC, NS, NB, PEI; adults exempt in Ontario
laws.fullDescription: Bicycle helmet requirements vary by province. British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and PEI require helmets for all cyclists. Ontario requires helmets only for cyclists under 18. Quebec has no provincial adult helmet law. E-bikes are categorized: power-assisted bicycles (max 32km/h, 500W) allowed on most roads without registration. Higher-speed electric bikes require registration and insurance. Cycling under the influence of alcohol or drugs can result in charges.
laws.penalty: $100-$250 fines in provinces with mandatory adult helmet laws
laws.exceptions: Religious head coverings accommodated in some jurisdictions

quiz.q: Bicycle helmet and cycling regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Explosives Act — Fireworks and Explosive Permits
laws.subtitle: Consumer fireworks (18+); professional display fireworks require federal permit
laws.fullDescription: The Explosives Act (RSC 1985 c E-17) governs fireworks. Consumer fireworks (F1, F2 classes) are sold at retail with age restrictions (typically 18+). Professional display fireworks (F3) require a federal Explosives Regulatory Division permit and pyrotechnician certificate. Many municipalities ban or restrict fireworks use year-round or seasonally. Illegal import of unapproved fireworks at the border triggers seizure and criminal prosecution. Halloween and July 1 are peak enforcement periods.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for criminal violations of the Explosives Act; $1,000+ municipal bylaw fines
laws.exceptions: Licensed pyrotechnic operators with ERD permits; professional film and TV productions

quiz.q: Fireworks and explosives regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: WAPPRIITA — CITES Implementation (Wildlife Trade)
laws.subtitle: Importing CITES-listed species without permits is illegal; ivory and rhino horn prohibited
laws.fullDescription: WAPPRIITA (SC 1992 c 52) implements CITES in Canada. Importing, exporting, or interprovincially transporting listed wildlife or their products without permits is prohibited. This includes ivory, rhino horn, shark fins (banned commercially in Canada since 2019), certain orchids and cacti, and numerous animal products. CBSA officers inspect shipments. Ivory trading has been further restricted following Canadian CITES Conference of Parties commitments.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment; fines up to $300,000
laws.exceptions: Pre-convention specimens with documentation; personal effects exemption for small quantities

quiz.q: CITES wildlife trade restrictions in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Impact Assessment Act 2019 — Environmental Review of Major Projects
laws.subtitle: Mines, pipelines, and dams need federal assessment; skipping is prohibited
laws.fullDescription: The Impact Assessment Act (SC 2019 c 28) requires designated major projects (mines, pipelines, dams, nuclear facilities) to undergo federal impact assessment. The Supreme Court ruled parts of the Act unconstitutional in 2023 as intruding on provincial jurisdiction; Parliament amended it with a more targeted federal nexus test. Projects that proceed without required assessment face injunctions. The IAA also requires consideration of Indigenous rights and climate impacts.
laws.penalty: Up to $500,000/day fines for commencing projects without required assessment
laws.exceptions: Designated projects with provincial equivalency agreements; emergency situations

quiz.q: Federal environmental assessment in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Fisheries Act — Recreational Fishing Licences
laws.subtitle: Licence required in all provinces; catch limits strictly enforced
laws.fullDescription: Recreational fishing in Canada requires either a provincial/territorial licence (for provincial waters) or a National Angling Licence for federal waters. Non-resident fees can reach $80/year in BC. Catch limits, minimum size restrictions, and prohibited methods (snagging, use of gill nets) are enforced by DFO Conservation and Protection officers and provincial enforcement. Fishing without a licence in national parks is prosecuted under both the Fisheries Act and the National Parks Act.
laws.penalty: Fines up to $100,000 for Fisheries Act violations; seizure of catch and equipment
laws.exceptions: Indigenous peoples exercising treaty rights; children under specified ages in some provinces

quiz.q: Recreational fishing licence requirements in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Customs Act — Undeclared Goods and Personal Exemptions
laws.subtitle: CAD $200 after 24h; $800 after 48h; undeclared goods subject to seizure
laws.fullDescription: The Customs Act (RSC 1985 c 1) requires all goods entering Canada to be declared. Personal exemptions apply: CAD $200 duty-free after 24 hours abroad, $800 after 48 hours. Tobacco (200 cigarettes) and alcohol (1.14L spirits or 1.5L wine) have separate allowances. Smuggling prohibited goods (firearms, drugs, CITES-listed wildlife) is a criminal offence. CBSA officers may search vehicles, luggage, and electronic devices without a warrant at the border.
laws.penalty: Seizure of goods; 25%-50% duty on undeclared goods; criminal charges for smuggling
laws.exceptions: Personal exemption thresholds; duty-free shop purchases within allowances

quiz.q: Customs and import declaration obligations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Possession of Break-in Tools (s.351)
laws.subtitle: Possessing lock picks or break-in tools without lawful excuse is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 351 of the Criminal Code makes possession of instruments designed for breaking and entering — lock picks, skeleton keys, slim jims, or similar devices — without lawful excuse a criminal offence. Locksmiths and security professionals carry authorization documentation. Being found near a break-in scene with such instruments significantly strengthens prosecution. Possession of a master key for vehicles (used in car theft) has been prosecuted under this section.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment
laws.exceptions: Licensed locksmiths with professional identification; security industry professionals with documentation

quiz.q: Possession of break-in instruments in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Arson (s.433-436)
laws.subtitle: Arson with disregard for human life carries life imprisonment; wildfire risk prosecuted severely
laws.fullDescription: Sections 433-436 of the Criminal Code address arson. Arson with disregard for human life carries life imprisonment. Fraudulent arson (insurance fraud) carries up to 10 years. Given Canada's catastrophic wildfire seasons — including the 2023 Yellowknife evacuation (20,000 residents) and the 2016 Fort McMurray fire (88,000 evacuated) — setting fires negligently in wildfire-prone areas is aggressively prosecuted. Provincial open burning permits and seasonal bans are strictly enforced.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment for arson with disregard for human life; 14 years for arson causing bodily harm
laws.exceptions: Legally authorized controlled burns with proper provincial permits

quiz.q: Arson offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Assault Causing Bodily Harm (s.267-268)
laws.subtitle: Assault with weapon: up to 10 years; aggravated assault: up to 14 years
laws.fullDescription: Section 267 makes assault with a weapon or causing bodily harm punishable by up to 10 years. Aggravated assault (wounding, maiming, disfiguring, or endangering life) under s.268 carries up to 14 years. Sexual assault with bodily harm: up to 14 years. Spousal assault is prosecuted proactively in Canada — police have a mandatory charge policy in many provinces when there is evidence of domestic assault regardless of whether the victim wishes to press charges.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years for assault causing bodily harm; up to 14 years for aggravated assault
laws.exceptions: Self-defence within proportionate limits (s.34 Criminal Code)

quiz.q: Assault causing bodily harm in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Canada Labour Code — Right to Strike (Part I)
laws.subtitle: Federal workers may strike after conciliation; essential services may be limited
laws.fullDescription: Part I of the Canada Labour Code governs collective bargaining for federally regulated industries (airlines, rail, banking, telecom). Workers must exhaust conciliation and mediation before a legal strike. Essential services designations may limit strikes (air traffic controllers, port workers). The Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) oversees disputes. Parliament has used back-to-work legislation in contentious disputes (Canada Post 2018, ports 2023).
laws.penalty: Illegal strikes result in contempt of court orders and union fines
laws.exceptions: Essential services designations; management and supervisory personnel

quiz.q: The right to strike for federal workers in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Employment Equity Act — Federally Regulated Employers
laws.subtitle: Federal employers with 100+ employees must promote diversity for four designated groups
laws.fullDescription: The Employment Equity Act (SC 1995 c 44) requires federally regulated private sector employers with 100+ employees to implement employment equity plans for four designated groups: women, Aboriginal peoples, persons with disabilities, and visible minorities. Employers must identify underrepresentation, set goals, and post plans. A 2022 review recommended expanding the Act's coverage and modernizing the designated group definitions to include 2SLGBTQI+ persons.
laws.penalty: Orders to develop equity plans; fines for non-compliance with reporting requirements
laws.exceptions: Federal public service covered by separate Public Service Employment Act provisions

quiz.q: Employment equity requirements in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Income Tax Act — Employment Withholding and CRA Compliance
laws.subtitle: All Canadian employment income must be reported; tax evasion is criminal
laws.fullDescription: The Income Tax Act (RSC 1985 c 1 5th Supp) requires employers to deduct income tax, CPP contributions, and EI premiums from wages and remit them to CRA. Foreign workers earning Canadian employment income must file Canadian tax returns. The CRA aggressively pursues unreported cash income — both employer and employee face criminal tax evasion charges for deliberate evasion. Canada-US tax treaty reduces double taxation for cross-border workers.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 5 years imprisonment; civil penalties 50%-200% of unpaid tax; interest
laws.exceptions: Basic personal amounts and various credits reduce tax; tax treaties for non-residents

quiz.q: Employment income tax obligations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Wiretapping and Private Communications (s.184)
laws.subtitle: Recording private conversations without consent or judicial authorization is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 184 of the Criminal Code makes wilfully intercepting private communications an indictable offence. Canada requires only one-party consent for recording — a participant in a conversation may record it. Two-party consent is not required federally (unlike some US states). However, recording without being a party, or recording for a criminal purpose, remains criminal. Employers recording employee communications without disclosure face criminal and civil liability.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment for unlawful interception
laws.exceptions: One-party consent recording; lawful judicial authorization for police wiretaps; 911 call recordings

quiz.q: Wiretapping and interception laws in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Assisted Human Reproduction Act — Prohibitions
laws.subtitle: Commercial surrogacy, cloning, and selling gametes are prohibited in Canada
laws.fullDescription: The Assisted Human Reproduction Act (SC 2004 c 2) prohibits human cloning, sex selection for non-medical reasons, creating embryos for research, and paying surrogates beyond reimbursement of actual documented expenses. Commercial surrogacy is illegal; altruistic surrogacy is legal. The Supreme Court ruled portions of the Act unconstitutional in 2010, returning some jurisdiction to provinces. Quebec, Ontario, and BC have provincial ART legislation. Purchasing sperm or eggs for compensation is illegal.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment for prohibited activities including human cloning
laws.exceptions: Altruistic surrogacy with documented expense reimbursement; licensed fertility clinics

quiz.q: Human cloning and commercial surrogacy prohibitions fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Chemical and Biological Weapons — Criminal Code and CWC
laws.subtitle: Development or possession of WMDs carries life imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: The Criminal Code and the Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act (SC 1995 c 25) make it criminal to develop, produce, stockpile, or use biological or chemical weapons. Canada is a signatory to the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological Weapons Convention. Unauthorized possession of Select Agents (dangerous pathogens: anthrax, botulinum toxin, smallpox) is prosecuted federally. Canada participates in OPCW verification missions.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment for weapons of mass destruction offences
laws.exceptions: Legitimate scientific research with Public Health Agency biosafety permits; industrial chemical use within regulatory limits

quiz.q: Chemical and biological weapons offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Safe Drinking Water — Provincial Regulation
laws.subtitle: Provinces enforce water quality; boil water advisories legally binding; First Nations reserve issues
laws.fullDescription: Drinking water regulation is primarily provincial in Canada. Ontario's Safe Drinking Water Act, BC's Drinking Water Protection Act, and similar laws set testing requirements. First Nations reserves on federal lands have historically had inadequate water systems — Canada committed to eliminating long-term drinking water advisories and largely succeeded by 2025 (down from 30+ in 2015). Violations of boil water advisories are public health offences under provincial legislation.
laws.penalty: Provincial fines up to $250,000 for water system operators who violate standards
laws.exceptions: Private wells on non-shared property often less regulated at provincial level

quiz.q: Drinking water safety regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Zero Emission Vehicle Mandate — Federal Standards
laws.subtitle: 20% ZEV sales required by 2026; 100% by 2035 for new passenger vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Electric Vehicle Availability Standard requires that zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs — battery electric, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen fuel cell) make up 20% of new passenger car and light truck sales by model year 2026, scaling to 100% by 2035. Several provinces (Quebec, BC) have their own ZEV mandates with province-specific credits. The federal Energy Efficiency Regulations also set fuel consumption standards for new vehicles.
laws.penalty: Compliance credits system; fines for manufacturers who fail to meet fleet standards
laws.exceptions: Small manufacturers; specialized vehicles with temporary exemptions

quiz.q: Canada's ZEV mandate falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Competition Act — Price Fixing and Anti-trust
laws.subtitle: Price-fixing cartels and bid rigging are per se criminal; up to 14 years imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: The Competition Act (RSC 1985 c C-34) makes price-fixing, market allocation, output restriction, and bid rigging criminal per se (no need to prove harm to competition). The Competition Bureau investigates and refers criminal matters to the DPP. Amendments in 2022 and 2024 strengthened merger review and added private rights of action for damages. Canada cooperates with US DOJ and EU Commission on international cartel investigations. Immunity program for cartel whistleblowers.
laws.penalty: Up to 14 years imprisonment; up to $25 million per offence for corporations
laws.exceptions: None for hard-core cartel behaviour; legitimate joint ventures may be permitted

quiz.q: Price fixing and cartel offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) — Strict Eligibility
laws.subtitle: Legal since 2016 Carter SCC decision; mental illness as sole condition deferred to 2027
laws.fullDescription: Canada legalized Medical Assistance in Dying in 2016 following Carter v Canada (SCC). Criminal Code exempts qualified practitioners following the MAID framework. Track 1 MAID (natural death reasonably foreseeable) and Track 2 MAID (not reasonably foreseeable but serious irreversible illness) have different safeguards. Eligibility based on mental illness as the sole underlying condition was twice deferred and is expected in March 2027. Over 13,000 MAID deaths occurred in 2022.
laws.penalty: Criminal liability for practitioners who fail to follow the Code framework
laws.exceptions: Children ineligible; mental illness sole condition deferred; waiting periods vary

quiz.q: Medical Assistance in Dying regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Canada Health Act — Public Health Insurance for Residents
laws.subtitle: Visitors NOT covered by provincial Medicare; travel insurance essential
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Medicare is administered by provinces under the Canada Health Act (RSC 1985 c C-6) on five principles: public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability, and accessibility. Foreign visitors are NOT covered by provincial health insurance and must have travel insurance or pay out-of-pocket. Emergency room visits cost $800-$3,000+ without insurance. New residents typically wait 3 months for provincial coverage. Some provinces (BC, Manitoba) eliminated the waiting period.
laws.penalty: Hospitals charge uninsured visitors full cost; emergency stabilization provided but billing follows
laws.exceptions: Emergency stabilization is provided regardless; provincial insurance for new residents after waiting period

quiz.q: Canada's public health insurance system falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: CSIS Act — National Security Intelligence
laws.subtitle: CSIS investigates threats to national security; foreign interference investigations active
laws.fullDescription: The Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act (RSC 1985 c C-23) establishes CSIS and authorizes investigation of threats including espionage, sabotage, foreign interference, and terrorism. CSIS requires Federal Court warrants for intrusive surveillance. A 2024 public inquiry found CSIS did not adequately brief political parties on Chinese interference in 2019 and 2021 elections. The National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians (NSICOP) provides parliamentary oversight.
laws.penalty: Criminal referrals to RCMP; no direct CSIS detention powers
laws.exceptions: Lawful advocacy, protest, and dissent; journalism and academic research

quiz.q: National security intelligence law in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Citizenship Act — Dual Citizenship Permitted
laws.subtitle: Canada allows dual citizenship; Canadian citizens must enter on Canadian passport
laws.fullDescription: Canada's Citizenship Act (RSC 1985 c C-29) permits dual or multiple citizenship. Canadians do not lose citizenship by acquiring another nationality. However, since 2016, Canadian citizens who also hold another passport must use their Canadian passport when boarding flights to Canada (tied to eTA rules). Citizenship revocation is only possible for fraud in the application process or treason. The Strengthening Canadian Citizenship Act (Bill C-24) provisions on revocation for terrorism were largely struck down.
laws.penalty: Fines for misrepresentation on citizenship applications; citizenship revocation for proven fraud
laws.exceptions: Natural-born citizens; dual citizens who comply with entry requirements

quiz.q: Dual citizenship rules in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Tobacco and Vaping Products Act — Age Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Federal minimum age 18 to purchase tobacco or vaping; most provinces require 19
laws.fullDescription: The Tobacco and Vaping Products Act (SC 1997 c 13) prohibits sales of tobacco or vaping products to persons under 18 federally. Most provinces set the minimum age at 19 (to align with legal drinking age). Canada bans flavoured vaping products that appeal to youth (except menthol/mint until 2023 then prohibited in most provinces). Plain packaging for tobacco has been mandatory since 2019. Smoking in federally regulated workplaces is banned under the Non-Smokers Health Act.
laws.penalty: Fines for retailers selling to underage buyers; compliance orders for manufacturers
laws.exceptions: Tobacco grown for personal use by farmers; ceremonial use by Indigenous peoples
laws.sourceLabel: Tobacco and Vaping Products Act SC 1997

quiz.q: Tobacco and vaping product regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Mischief and Property Damage (s.430)
laws.subtitle: Wilfully damaging property, graffiti, and interfering with data are criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 430 of the Criminal Code defines mischief as wilfully destroying or damaging property, obstructing its lawful use, or obstructing computer data. Graffiti is prosecuted under mischief provisions. Mischief causing over $5,000 damage carries up to 10 years; under $5,000, up to 2 years. Mischief to cultural property (monuments, places of worship) carries enhanced penalties. The 2022 Ottawa Freedom Convoy blockade resulted in mischief charges against organizers.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years for mischief over $5,000; life imprisonment if death results
laws.exceptions: Lawful demolition with permit; property owner damaging own property if no third-party endangerment

quiz.q: Mischief and property damage offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Theft and Shoplifting (s.334)
laws.subtitle: Theft over $5,000 up to 10 years; shoplifting creates a criminal record affecting travel
laws.fullDescription: Section 334 distinguishes theft over $5,000 (indictable, up to 10 years) from theft under $5,000 (hybrid, up to 2 years on indictment). Shoplifting creates a criminal record which can impact employment, professional licences, and US travel. Retailers may detain suspected shoplifters under citizens' arrest provisions (s.494 Criminal Code). The Bank of Montreal Arena organized retail crime task force prosecutes organized shoplifting rings under conspiracy charges.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years for theft over $5,000; up to 2 years for theft under $5,000
laws.exceptions: Claim of right — genuine belief property is one's own

quiz.q: Theft and shoplifting offences in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Pest Control Products Act — Pesticide Regulation
laws.subtitle: Only Health Canada-registered pesticides may be used; herbicides in US may not be legal here
laws.fullDescription: The Pest Control Products Act (SC 2002 c 28) requires all pesticides to be registered by Health Canada's PMRA before sale or use. Several pesticides legal in the US (certain neonicotinoids, atrazine at high concentrations) are restricted or banned in Canada. Provinces may have stricter restrictions. Homeowners, farmers, and landscapers must follow label directions — off-label use is illegal. Cosmetic pesticide bans in Ontario and Quebec restrict residential lawn pesticide use.
laws.penalty: Up to $1 million fines for corporate violations; up to $500,000 for individuals
laws.exceptions: Registered products used per label instructions; emergency pest control with PMRA emergency registration

quiz.q: Pesticide regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Corporate Criminal Liability (Bill C-45)
laws.subtitle: Corporations can be criminally liable for workplace safety failures causing death
laws.fullDescription: Bill C-45 (2004) amended the Criminal Code to create corporate criminal liability for workplace safety failures. Following the 1992 Westray Mine disaster (26 miners killed), Section 217.1 requires organizations to take reasonable steps to prevent bodily harm to workers and the public. Criminal negligence causing death or bodily harm in a workplace context can result in criminal conviction of the corporation and individuals involved (directors, supervisors).
laws.penalty: Criminal conviction of corporation; unlimited fines; individual managers up to life imprisonment
laws.exceptions: Regulatory (non-criminal) prosecution under OHS legislation is more common for less egregious violations

quiz.q: Corporate liability for workplace safety failures in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Discharge of Firearm Recklessly (s.244.2)
laws.subtitle: Drive-by shooting or reckless discharge in occupied areas carries up to 14 years
laws.fullDescription: Section 244.2 of the Criminal Code creates the offence of intentionally discharging a firearm while being reckless about whether the discharge would endanger life or safety of another person in a place frequented by people. Added in response to gang-related drive-by shootings in Toronto and Vancouver. Minimum 4 years if gang-related. Canada's Major Crime Units coordinate with US agencies on cross-border gang activity.
laws.penalty: Up to 14 years; minimum 4 years if associated with criminal organization
laws.exceptions: Lawful self-defence within proportionate limits; accidental discharge may lack requisite intent

quiz.q: Reckless firearm discharge in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Kidnapping and Unlawful Confinement (s.279-281)
laws.subtitle: Kidnapping carries up to life imprisonment; child abduction separately prosecuted
laws.fullDescription: Sections 279-281 address kidnapping, forcible confinement, and hostage-taking. Kidnapping carries up to life imprisonment. Unlawful confinement carries up to 10 years. Child abduction by a parent in violation of a custody order (s.282-283) carries up to 10 years. Canada cooperates with Interpol on international parental abduction under the Hague Convention on Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. Hostage-taking is an aggravated form carrying life.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment for kidnapping; up to 10 years for unlawful confinement
laws.exceptions: Lawful arrest by peace officer; lawful detention under court order

quiz.q: Kidnapping and unlawful confinement in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Obstruction of Justice (s.139)
laws.subtitle: Intimidating witnesses, destroying evidence, or bribing jurors is criminal
laws.fullDescription: Section 139 makes it an indictable offence to obstruct, pervert, or defeat the course of justice. This includes intimidating witnesses, bribing jurors, destroying evidence, and lying to police in material ways during investigations. Obstruction of a peace officer (s.129) — including providing a false name — is a hybrid offence. High-profile Canadian obstruction prosecutions have involved politicians, executives, and organized crime members. Victim intimidation by accused persons triggers additional charges.
laws.penalty: Up to 10 years for obstruction of justice; up to 2 years for obstruction of peace officer
laws.exceptions: Legitimate exercise of legal rights; refusing to answer questions while waiting for counsel

quiz.q: Obstruction of justice in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Weed Control and Invasive Species — Provincial Legislation
laws.subtitle: Spreading invasive species is prohibited; Garlic mustard, Purple Loosestrife etc controlled
laws.fullDescription: All Canadian provinces have weed control and invasive species legislation. Ontario's Invasive Species Act (2015) designates prohibited species (Giant Hogweed, Phragmites, Asian carp) that cannot be possessed, sold, or released. Boaters must clean, drain, and dry watercraft before moving between water bodies to prevent spread of zebra mussels and other aquatic invaders. Garlic mustard, Japanese knotweed, and burning bush are restricted in many jurisdictions.
laws.penalty: Fines $200-$100,000 for possessing or releasing prohibited invasive species
laws.exceptions: Research under permit; natural occurrences before legislation

quiz.q: Invasive species regulations in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Impersonation (s.402.2-403)
laws.subtitle: Identity theft and fraudulently personating another person are criminal
laws.fullDescription: Sections 402.2 and 403 of the Criminal Code address identity theft (obtaining another's identity information to commit an indictable offence) and identity fraud (personating someone else to gain advantage). Canada ranks among countries with high rates of identity fraud; CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) identity theft via My Account compromises have resulted in millions in fraudulent tax refunds. RCMP and provincial police coordinate with international agencies on identity theft rings.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years for identity theft (s.402.2); up to 10 years for identity fraud (s.403)
laws.exceptions: Authorized undercover police operations; performers using stage names with disclosure

quiz.q: Identity theft and fraud in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Residential Tenancies — Provincial Landlord-Tenant Protection
laws.subtitle: Each province has its own residential tenancy legislation; rent control in some
laws.fullDescription: Residential tenancy is provincially regulated in Canada. Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act covers buildings built before 2018 under rent control (max annual increase tied to inflation). BC's RTA limits rent increases to CPI + 2%. Quebec has a Tribunal administratif du logement. Evictions require Landlord and Tenant Board hearings in most provinces. Security deposits are limited (one month in many provinces) or prohibited (Quebec). Foreign visitors renting AirBnBs are protected under the same legislation.
laws.penalty: Fines for illegal lockouts; orders to return illegal deposits; rent abatements
laws.exceptions: Owner-occupied co-ops; seasonal and tourist accommodations; some exempt categories

quiz.q: Landlord-tenant protections in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Causing Disturbance (s.175)
laws.subtitle: Fighting in public, shouting obscenities, or disturbing the peace are criminal offences
laws.fullDescription: Section 175 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence to cause a disturbance in or near a public place by fighting, screaming, shouting, swearing, singing, or using insulting or obscene language. Being intoxicated in a public place is a provincial or territorial offence (not federal Criminal Code) in most Canadian jurisdictions. Creating a disturbance is a summary conviction offence but results in a criminal record. Police have significant discretion in charging.
laws.penalty: Summary conviction — up to $2,000 fine and/or 6 months imprisonment
laws.exceptions: Lawful picket lines; authorized public demonstrations; artistic performances with permits

quiz.q: Causing a public disturbance in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Canada Shipping Act — Marine Pollution Prohibition
laws.subtitle: Discharging oil, sewage, or garbage from vessels in Canadian waters is prohibited
laws.fullDescription: The Canada Shipping Act 2001 (SC 2001 c 26) regulates vessel operations and prohibits discharging pollutants (oil, sewage, garbage) in Canadian waters. MARPOL requirements are implemented domestically. Transport Canada and the Coast Guard enforce compliance. Pleasure craft operators must not dump holding tank waste in fresh water bodies. The Act also requires vessels in the Arctic to meet enhanced pollution prevention standards under NORDREG.
laws.penalty: Up to $1 million fines for corporations; up to $50,000 for individuals
laws.exceptions: Emergency discharge to save life; authorized discharge in approved areas far from shore

quiz.q: Marine pollution laws in Canada fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under environmental law.

laws.title: Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act — Whistleblower Protection
laws.subtitle: Federal public servants who report wrongdoing are protected from reprisal
laws.fullDescription: The Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act (SC 2005 c 46) protects federal public servants who disclose wrongdoing (breaches of law, gross mismanagement, abuse of authority, imminent danger) to supervisors or the Integrity Commissioner. Protected disclosures cannot result in reprisal. The Integrity Commissioner investigates and recommends remedies. BC, Ontario, and other provinces have complementary provincial public sector whistleblower legislation.
laws.penalty: Reprisal against a whistleblower is a disciplinary offence; reinstatement and compensation ordered
laws.exceptions: Disclosures solely for personal gain; disclosures of Cabinet confidences

quiz.q: Whistleblower protection in Canadian federal employment falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under labor law.

laws.title: Criminal Code — Impersonating a Police Officer (s.130)
laws.subtitle: Wearing a police uniform or impersonating an officer is a criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Section 130 of the Criminal Code makes impersonating a peace officer (police, customs officer, constable) or wearing a uniform that could be mistaken for police a criminal offence. Using a fake badge or claiming police authority to gain compliance or access is criminal even without a uniform. CRA phone fraud and RCMP impersonation scams targeting newcomers and seniors have increased; being a victim of such scams is not illegal but reporting promptly is encouraged.
laws.penalty: Up to 5 years imprisonment
laws.exceptions: Theatrical performances clearly identified as entertainment; costume events

quiz.q: Impersonating a police officer in Canada falls under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under criminal law.

laws.title: Accessible Parking — DPP Misuse is an Offence
laws.subtitle: Using disabled parking permits without eligibility results in fines up to $5,000
laws.fullDescription: Provinces issue Disabled Parking Permits (DPPs) to persons with mobility disabilities. Misusing a DPP — using another person's permit, using a deceased person's permit, or parking in accessible spaces without a valid DPP — is an offence under provincial Highway Traffic Acts. Ontario increased DPP misuse fines to $5,000 in 2016 to deter abuse. Accessible parking spaces are required in lots above minimum size by building codes.
laws.penalty: $300-$5,000 fines for DPP misuse; same range for parking in accessible space without permit
laws.exceptions: DPP holders using any designated accessible parking space; emergency situations

quiz.q: Disabled parking permit rules fall under which legal category?
quiz.explanation: This law falls under traffic law.

laws.title: Oceans Act — Marine Protected Areas
laws.subtitle: Fishing, anchoring, and pollution prohibited in MPAs; whale watching has minimum distances
